name: Kikuyu
confidence_why: Four first-hand descriptions (Hinde 1904, McGregor 1905, Barlow 1914 and Armstrong 1940, the standard phonetic study of the language) all put a weak stress on the penultimate syllable, and the one dissent, Philippson 1991, is a comparative survey that files Kikuyu as purely tonal, a statement about the type of prosodic system that does not place the stress anywhere else.

catalog_quote: STRESS. Main Stress. The general rule is that the last syllable but one (penultimate syllable) bears the main accent, though frequently the stress is so light as to be scarcely distinguishable. Exs. nyũ'mba; kĩhā'to; nĩngamwo'na; gũthiũrũrũ'ka. Effect of Suffix. The stress may be shifted because of the addition of a suffix or suffixes. Ex. ako'me, akoma'ge, akomagĩ're. Effect of Monosyllables. In certain cases a word of one syllable following another word is closely joined to it in pronunciation and causes the accent to fall on the last syllable of that word. ... Syllable consisting of Vowel only. In Kikuyu, a syllable consisting of a vowel only, always tends to be absorbed by the preceding syllable; so that when the last syllable of a word consists of a vowel only, the stress is generally on the third last syllable (antepenultimate), not on the second last. In such words as kũ-rĩ-a, a-ge-ri-e, kwe-ndi-o, the accentuation is ... kũ'-rĩ-a, a-ge'-ri-e, kwe'-ndi-o, the -rĩa, -rie, and -ndio, being treated as single syllables. NOTE. There are a number of exceptions to this rule, e.g., ĩtĩ'a, be conceited; iri'a, milk; the tense forms of the verbs thi'ĩ, go; gĩ'a, have; tu'a, break; &c. ... Sometimes the main stress may be changed from the penultimate position in interrogation. [p.7] ... The above rules being only general and exceptions numerous all important deviations are marked in the vocabularies in this book by the usual stress sign.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kikuyu is not in the catalog. Of the five title hits, only Philippson 1991 (Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East Bantu) is about this language's prosody; it is print-only (theses.fr 'accessible: non'), and its abstract classes Kikuyu as 'pleinement tonale' at the opposite pole from penultimate-demarcative-accent languages like Swahili — a mild tension with the older grammars. Wagacha et al. 2006 (downloaded, read) is orthographic diacritic restoration with no prosody content; Dybo 1994, Feldstein 1978 and Kiparsky 2010 are Saharan/Slavic/Indo-European accentology attached to Kikuyu by Glottolog's computerized keyword 'paradigmatic' (Dybo's record says so explicitly). Best first-hand statement read: Barlow 1914 p.6 (page scan verified) — weak penultimate main stress, final vowel-only syllable absorbed so surface antepenult, shifts under suffixes/enclitics/emphasis; corroborated by McGregor 1905, Hinde 1904 and the Armstrong 1940 §516 snippet already held by the project. Acquisition list of works to obtain: Armstrong 1940 ch. XXIII (snippet only) and Philippson 1991 (medium).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak main stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (recomputed over the whole word as suffixes are added); where the word ends in a bare-vowel syllable (…C V-V), that vowel is absorbed into the preceding syllable so stress surfaces on the antepenult; stress is independent of the (contrastive) tone system and is often barely perceptible. Corroborated by McGregor 1905 p.13 ('In the majority of cases the accent falls on the penultimate syllable') and by Armstrong 1940 section 516 (snippet: 'A weak stress occurs generally on the penultimate syllable, and is independent of tone… often so weak that… it is impossible to distinguish it').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described (Barlow speaks only of 'main stress'/'main accent').
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions to the vowel-absorption (antepenult) sub-rule: ĩtĩ'a 'be conceited', iri'a 'milk', tense forms of thi'ĩ 'go', gĩ'a 'have', tu'a 'break', &c; a closely joined following monosyllable draws the accent onto the final syllable of the preceding word (Ikara' thĩ; akĩĩgi'ta na' ngo); stress 'freely changed in conversation for the sake of emphasis and rhetorical effect', often with vowel lengthening; 'Sometimes the main stress may be changed from the penultimate position in interrogation' (p.6-7); enclitics rĩ and ĩ 'do not usually affect the position of the stress' (p.8); 'The above rules being only general and exceptions numerous all important deviations are marked in the vocabularies' (p.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on citation forms, but with phrase-level perturbations (following monosyllables, emphasis, interrogation). Kikuyu is a two-tone + downstep language (Armstrong 1940; Clements 1984; Englebretson & Wa-Ngatho 2015); all three sources that mention stress (McGregor 1905, Barlow 1914, Armstrong 1940 snippet) call it weak/light and penultimate, and modern descriptions discuss tone only.
new_statements.identity_note: Barlow 1914 describes Kikuyu as used at the Church of Scotland mission (standard orthography of the United Kikuyu Language Committee); no dialect is singled out, so it maps to kiku1240 at language level. McGregor 1905 (CMS) likewise language-level. Githinji 2014 (silent on stress) is specifically the Ki-Ndia dialect (Kirinyaga). Armstrong 1940 is based on one educated speaker (per Clements 1984).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kikuyu is analysed as a purely tonal language (H/L with lexical contour tones, 10 patterns on disyllabic noun stems, post-lexical rightward tone shift). Unlike its close relatives Kamba and Chaga it has no demarcative accent and no lexical accent opposition in noun stems (p.374 'le kikuyu ne connaît pas de différence d'accentuation dans ses thèmes nominaux'), and the penultimate syllable carries no culmination of pitch, length or intensity and plays no role in tone association: 'statut de la pénultième: néant'. The only penult-related fact noted is intonational (a realised rising tone occurs only on the penultimate of an utterance in certain intonational contexts, p.378). Nothing is said about a weak expiratory stress of the Armstrong/Barlow kind; Philippson's parameters (§3.5.1) are culmination of pitch, length or intensity, and he finds none on the Kikuyu penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none discussed (no accent at all is posited for Kikuyu)
new_statements.exceptions: Imperatives without a complement exceptionally escape tone shift (r&E:hE ! 'apporte !', p.451 n.1), which the author links to intonation; rising tones surface only on an utterance-penultimate syllable in some intonational contexts (p.378). Kamba (not Kikuyu) has a partly free lexical accent, penultimate vs final.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Kikuyu data are Central Kikuyu (standard Gĩkũyũ as in Clements 1984 and Armstrong 1940; group XXII 'Thagicu / Kenya Central' with Kamba); no dialect is singled out. Mugane 1997 describes standard Gĩkũyũ (not opened).

tone_statements.quote: Kikuyu is a tone language with an underlying /H L Ø/ tonal distinction and with rising and falling contour tones.1 The syllable is the Tone Bearing Unit (TBU) and every TBU in Kikuyu has a surface tone. ... The underlying Ø tones are annotated with a L tone on the surface. ... Kikuyu attests a number of tone rules. The ones relevant for this study are High Tone Spreading (HTS), NON-FINALITY and floating L tones which trigger downstep (ꜜ) on surface H and L tones in specific syntactic configurations.
tone_statements.summary: Underlying H vs L plus toneless Ø (surfaces as L); rising and falling contours also occur; total downstep (one-level drop) on both H and L, triggered by two floating L tones at the phrase edge.

tone_statements.quote: In Kikuyu, tone association is fully predictable (Clements & Ford 1979, Clements 1984): the first tone is associated with the first two syllables, and each subsequent tone is associated with the syllable immediately following the morpheme that supplied it. ... Kikuyu allows rising tones on the final syllable ... Kikuyu does not allow contour tones falling from H to L̄ ( = extra low). As a result, the L̄ tone remains floating in (5), where its presence can be inferred from its role in the downstep system (Clements & Ford 1979: 203ff.)

tone_statements.translation: Accent is not written in the orthography, but here vowels (and preconsonantal nasals) pronounced high are marked with ´, and when a rising pitch is to be shown ˇ is added; transcriptions that abstract away from accent are given in italics. ... For example, kūgūrū 'leg', pronounced on its own, is kūgūrū, low and level, but before nī 'is' it becomes kúgúrú nī... ('the leg is ...'), high and level, and standing after nī it becomes ní kúgūrū. Thus one and the same noun appears in accentually different shapes according to the context in which it occurs.

readall_conflicts: Only one of the three works yields anything, and only as an abstract: Philippson 1991 classes Kikuyu as a 'purely tonal' system at the opposite pole from demarcative penultimate stress, which is a typological disagreement with the catalog's fixed-penultimate record. It is not a placement conflict: the first-hand sources already held by the project (Barlow 1914 p.6, McGregor 1905 p.13, Hinde 1904 p.ix, and Armstrong 1940 §516 in snippet) all put a weak, non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable and Armstrong states it is independent of tone, so Philippson's classification is about the prosodic system type (tone, not accent), which is compatible with a phonetically weak penultimate stress. Mugane 1997 could not be opened (lending-only) and Cysouw 2001 is not about Kikuyu. Philippson 1991 (full text now read) files Kikuyu as a purely tonal language with no demarcative accent and states that the penultimate syllable plays no role whatsoever (ch.6 §3.5.2(e) p.485; annexe pp.513-514 'statut de la pénultième: néant'), explicitly unlike Kamba and Chaga. This contradicts the catalog's classification of Kikuyu as fixed penultimate stress (Barlow 1914 p.6, corroborated by McGregor 1905 p.13, Hinde 1904 p.ix and the Armstrong 1940 §516 snippet). The disagreement is about type, not position: the older sources report a weak, non-contrastive penultimate stress 'so light as to be scarcely distinguishable' (Barlow) / 'often so weak that.. it is impossible to distinguish' (Armstrong)…
